conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in caring for new mothers in the weeks and months after birth, and I’m here to support you.

To help me understand how you’ve been feeling, I’d like to do a quick, routine screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s a simple 10-question form that looks at mood, anxiety, and how life with your baby has felt over the past seven days. It also includes a question about thoughts of self-harm so we can be sure you’re safe.

Everything you share stays confidential within our treatment team unless you tell me you plan to hurt yourself or someone else, or if there’s concern about a child’s safety. My goal is to create a comfortable, judgment-free space where you can be honest—there are no right or wrong answers, and many new moms find parts of this period harder than they expected.

We’ll go through each question one by one; you can answer in your own words, and I’ll jot down what you say. When we’re done I’ll add up the score and we can talk about what it means and any next steps that might help you feel better.

Does that sound all right? Ready to begin?

**First question:** Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Um… I guess? I mean, every now and then my partner will do something silly—like yesterday he tried to fold the stroller the wrong way and got his foot stuck—and I chuckled a little, but it feels kind of muted. Nothing really makes me laugh the way it used to. Mostly I’m just tired, so even when something’s funny, it feels like too much effort to really enjoy it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… like I said, I can still laugh a little, but it feels kind of distant—like I’m watching myself laugh instead of really feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I try to tell myself I should be excited about little plans—like my mom coming over to help or the baby’s bath time—but mostly I just feel kind of flat. I do them anyway, but it’s more going through the motions than actually looking forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like, if the baby won’t settle, I’ll catch myself thinking maybe I’m not doing something right—maybe I missed a hunger cue or waited too long to swaddle him. Rationally I know newborns are just fussy, but in the moment it feels like I must have messed up somehow. It’s not constant, though; just little flashes of “this is my fault.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… a few times a day I’ll suddenly feel my chest get tight, even when nothing’s happening. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly worry that the baby’s breathing has changed, or I’ll imagine him spitting up and choking when I’m not looking. I know it’s unlikely, but the thought just barges in and I can’t shake it for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of nights this week I woke up with my heart racing and this sudden rush of dread—like something awful was about to happen, even though the room was quiet and the baby was asleep in the bassinet. It only lasted a few minutes, but it felt like I couldn’t catch my breath. I hadn’t had anything like that before the baby came.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days I feel like I’m treading water. I’ll finally get him down for a nap and remember the sink’s full of bottles, or I’ll start a shower and hear him cry before I’m even wet. It’s not that any single thing is huge, but the pile just feels… heavy. I keep telling myself “tomorrow I’ll catch up,” but tomorrow’s the same loop.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not really that I feel wildly unhappy—it’s more that my brain won’t turn off. When I lie down, I replay every little sound he made during the day and wonder if I missed something important, or I fret about how I’ll manage tomorrow on so little rest. I fall asleep okay most nights, but I wake up at two or three and stare at the ceiling for an hour before I drift off again.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel kind of down some of the day—like a gray cloud that drifts in and out. It’s not there every minute, but when it shows up I just feel weepy and heavy, like I’m moving through molasses. Yesterday I put on music we used to love and I couldn’t even finish a song before I turned it off—I just didn’t have the heart for it.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really… I’ve teared up maybe once or twice this week, mostly when I’m extra tired, but it’s not an everyday thing. I just feel kind of numb more than anything, like the tears are stuck.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I might feel overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like “me” again and be able to enjoy my baby.

You described feeling emotionally distant from things that once brought joy, as though you're watching yourself laugh rather than genuinely feeling it. Daily worries about your baby's safety leave your chest tight even while folding laundry, and sudden nighttime panics have started waking you. You often feel like you're treading water: bottles pile up, showers get interrupted, and a "gray cloud" of sadness drifts in most days, making music feel pointless. Although you don't have thoughts of self-harm, you long to feel like "you" again and to enjoy your baby.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to genuinely laugh, describing emotional detachment from the experience, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent anhedonia—feeling "flat," "going through the motions," and unable to feel excitement even for positive events—aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intermittent self-blame "sometimes" and "some of the time," aligning directly with the "Yes, some of the time" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient experiences multiple intrusive, uncontrollable worry episodes daily that are clearly disproportionate and not triggered by real events, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden nighttime panic attacks with racing heart and dread, occurring multiple times this week without clear cause, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm ('most days') and inability to keep up, matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>Response describes frequent sadness that intrudes intermittently and disrupts enjoyment, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score of 18 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depression; your answers on items 2, 4, and 8 are scored at the maximum, reflecting severe anhedonia, frequent anxiety, and persistent low mood. These symptoms, coupled with middle insomnia, self-reported "gray cloud" sadness, and functional impairment (difficulty completing tasks, interrupted self-care), align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Absence of self-harm thoughts (item 10 score 0) means no immediate safety alert, but the overall pattern warrants urgent clinical assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss these results and consider medication or therapy options
2. Ask your provider for a referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for evaluation and possible <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> or other evidence-based treatment
3. Reach out to local <med>postpartum support groups</med> or telephone/online peer supports for shared experience and encouragement
4. Practise brief <med>breathing exercises</med> or <med>progressive muscle relaxation</med> when you notice chest tightness or panic
5. Enlist practical help: accept meals, delegate night feeds where possible, and prioritise two-hour rest blocks during the day to reduce sleep debt
6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track changes after interventions begin
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Post-delivery mother, approx. 1–2 weeks postpartum  
Date: [today]  
Screener: [Name, credentials]

Symptoms & Concerns  
- Anhedonia: marked reduction in ability to feel pleasure; describes laughter as “distant,” events as “flat.”  
- Persistent low mood: reports daily “gray cloud,” tearfulness, feeling “heavy.”  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame: attributes infant fussing to personal error despite cognitive awareness.  
- Generalized & peripartum-specific anxiety: daily intrusive worries about infant safety, chest tightness, middle-of-night panic episodes (2× this week).  
- Sleep disruption: initial insomnia not present; middle insomnia with rumination about infant care.  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed/treading water, difficulty completing tasks.  
- Denies suicidal ideation, self-harm thoughts, or intent.

Pattern Summary  
Consistent with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms with comorbid anxiety; functional impairment in self-care and task completion; no current safety risk.

Screening Significance  
Elevated score indicators for:  
– Postpartum depression (anhedonia, low mood, guilt, sleep disturbance)  
– Postpartum anxiety (panic-type awakenings, intrusive catastrophic worries)  

Risk Factors Present  
- Loss of pleasure/guilt  
- Middle insomnia tied to mood  
- Daily anxiety/panic not better explained by medical causes  
- Denies self-harm → safety concern absent at time of screen

Next Steps  
Recommend formal evaluation with EPDS/PHQ-9/GAD-7 and referral to perinatal mental health specialist for differential diagnosis and treatment planning. Monitor safety at all follow-ups.
